metadata.title: Pre-service teachers' perceptions of teacher morality in China

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study used a questionnaire survey and qualitative components with a single-institution sample (East China Normal University, Shanghai) of pre-service teachers in an M.Ed. programme. The manuscript reports descriptive statistics and multiple regression analyses (SPSS) but does not report the use of complex survey weights or any sampling/replicate-weight variables. Because the data are not drawn from an international ILSA sampling frame and no weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) is mentioned, weighting is treated as not applied/undocumented. The analytic sample is defined by completed questionnaires (N=203) and additional qualitative writings/interviews (81 writings; 13 interviewees), with no stated imputation or PV/scaling procedures typical of ILSA achievement assessments.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This paper does not analyze cognitive achievement scores with ILSA-style Plausible Values; instead, it models pre-service teachers’ perceptions of teacher morality and political-civic competences using Likert-scale questionnaire items and coded responses to dilemmas. Because the dependent variables are non-PV attitudinal/reflective measures (and qualitative codes), PV handling is not applicable by design. The manuscript also does not describe any missing-data strategy (e.g., complete-case rules or imputation), so missing-data handling is not reported.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study sampled pre-service teachers from the Master of Education (M.Ed.) programme at East China Normal University (ECNU) in Shanghai. Questionnaires were administered to Year One students (122 returned) and Year Two students (81 returned) across 13 majors, yielding 203 completed questionnaires with a 70% return rate. The quantitative analyses use the completed questionnaire responses (N=203) and the qualitative components include 81 written reports and 13 focus-group interview participants selected from different majors. The manuscript notes limited generalisability due to the restricted sample but does not specify additional exclusion criteria beyond completion/return.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS-based questionnaire items (adapted) — China (ECNU M.Ed. pre-service teachers, 2017-2018 survey)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multiple regression (controlling for background variables): R²=0.586; F(9,184)=28.905; p<.001. Significant predictors: PI (b=0.377, p<.001), SS (b=0.249, p<.001), LA (b=0.289, p<.01). Non-significant: PP (b=-0.061, p>.05); gender, teacher certification, normal school graduate, CCP membership, birthplace (all p>.05). N=203.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS-adapted questionnaire data from China (ECNU M.Ed. pre-service teachers, 2017-2018 survey), the study leveraged political identity, scientific spirit, and rule-of-law awareness to predict teacher morality perception, finding that these three political-civic competence perceptions significantly increased teacher morality perceptions (R²=0.586). This indicates that strengthening pre-service teachers’ political-civic competence components—especially rule-of-law awareness—may align their perceived teacher morality with state/CCP-regulated expectations, though the study is correlational and limited to a single-program sample.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS-based questionnaire items (adapted) — China (ECNU M.Ed. pre-service teachers, 2017-2018 survey)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multiple regression (controlling for background variables): R²=0.506; F(6,187)=31.894; p<.001. Significant predictors: teacher morality perception (b=0.695, p<.001) and CCP membership (b=-0.106, p<.05). Non-significant: gender, teacher certification, normal school graduate, birthplace (all p>.05). N=203.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS-adapted questionnaire data from China (ECNU M.Ed. pre-service teachers, 2017-2018 survey), the study leveraged teacher morality perception and CCP membership to predict political-civic competence perception, finding that teacher morality perception strongly increased political-civic competence perceptions (b=0.695, p<.001) while CCP membership had a smaller but significant negative association (b=-0.106, p<.05). This indicates that teacher morality and political-civic competence are tightly linked in pre-service teachers’ self-perceptions, suggesting teacher education should integrate moral-ethical reflection with civic-political learning, while noting that causality cannot be inferred from cross-sectional regression.

data.outcome_summary: This study surveyed 203 pre-service teachers in the ECNU Shanghai M.Ed. programme (2017–2018) using a questionnaire that included teacher-morality items and political-civic competence items adapted from ICCS (2009–2011) and related Chinese citizenship education work. The quantitative analysis used descriptive statistics and multiple regression (SPSS), not machine learning, to examine how political-civic competence perceptions relate to teacher morality perceptions and vice versa. For teacher morality perception, political identity (b=0.377), scientific spirit (b=0.249), and rule-of-law awareness (b=0.289) were significant predictors, with R²=0.586 (F(9,184)=28.905, p<.001). For political-civic competence perception, teacher morality perception was a strong predictor (b=0.695, p<.001) with R²=0.506 (F(6,187)=31.894, p<.001). The study is limited by its single-institution sample and by the absence of any reported missing-data strategy or PV/achievement scaling procedures.
